name: Guillain-Barré syndrome

matching.reasoningTemplate: Progressive ascending weakness with areflexia and no fever suggests Guillain-Barré; watch respiratory function.

redFlags: Respiratory failure & autonomic instability - monitor FVC, may need ventilation

clinicalPearls: About 70% of cases follow an acute infection (usually respiratory or GI) by 1-3 weeks; roughly 20-30% are preceded by Campylobacter jejuni, with a similar share after herpesvirus infection (often CMV or EBV) (p.3617).
Weakness usually evolves over hours to a few days and is classically ascending (legs more than arms), often first noticed as 'rubbery legs', with tingling dysesthesias in the extremities (p.3617).

Facial diparesis occurs in ~50% of patients and lower cranial nerve/bulbar involvement is common; bulbar weakness with difficulty handling secretions can initially be mistaken for brainstem ischemia (p.3617).
Pain (neck, shoulder, back, or diffuse spinal pain) is common early, in ~50% of patients, and deep aching muscle pain plus dysesthetic limb pain also occur (p.3617).
Large-fiber functions (deep tendon reflexes, proprioception) are affected more severely than cutaneous pain/temperature sensation (p.3617).

AMAN and AMSAN are axonal variants associated with anti-GD1a/anti-GM1 antibodies and preceding C. jejuni; AMAN can occur in seasonal outbreaks (e.g., rural China) and is prevalent in China and Mexico (p.3617-3619).
Miller Fisher syndrome (~5% of cases) presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia without limb weakness and carries anti-GQ1b antibodies in >90% (p.3617, p.3619).
If diagnosis is strongly suspected, treatment should not wait for the characteristic CSF or electrodiagnostic findings to evolve (p.3620).
harrison.pathophysiology: GBS is an acute, often fulminant autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy thought to arise from immune responses to non-self antigens (infections, vaccines) that cross-react with peripheral nerve via molecular mimicry, with gangliosides (glycosphingolipids concentrated at sites such as nodes of Ranvier) as likely targets. In AIDP, the demyelinating and most common form, both cellular and humoral mechanisms operate: complement deposits on the outer Schwann cell surface, triggering membrane-attack-complex formation, vesicular myelin disintegration, and macrophage-mediated removal of myelin. The resulting conduction block (with axons left intact) explains the flaccid paralysis and the potential for rapid recovery once remyelination occurs; secondary axonal degeneration in severe cases slows recovery and worsens residual deficit. In the axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN), IgG and complement deposit at the nodes of Ranvier of motor axons, with anti-GD1a antibodies preferentially targeting motor over sensory roots; low CMAP amplitudes often reflect reversible nodal/paranodal conduction block rather than true axon loss, though severe cases show axonal degeneration (p.3617-3620).
additionalDifferentials: Acute myelopathies, especially with prolonged back pain and sphincter disturbance (p.3620)
Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) in patients with late or recurrent relapses (p.3622)
infectionMimics: Poliomyelitis and acute flaccid myelitis (wild-type poliovirus, West Nile virus, enterovirus D68, enterovirus A71, Japanese encephalitis virus) (p.3620)
Lyme polyradiculitis and other tick-borne paralyses (p.3620)
Botulism (a neuromuscular junction disorder; pupillary reactivity lost early) (p.3620)
nonInfectiousMimics: Poisoning with organophosphates, thallium, or arsenic (p.3620)
additionalInvestigations: CSF protein may be normal when symptoms have been present <=48 h and usually rises only by the end of the first week, so a normal early CSF does not exclude GBS (p.3619).

A sustained CSF pleocytosis (or counts above the GBS range) should prompt a search for an alternative or concurrent diagnosis such as viral myelitis, HIV, leukemia/lymphoma infiltrating nerves, or neurosarcoidosis (p.3619).
Electrodiagnostic abnormalities are mild or absent early and lag behind the clinical course; earliest AIDP findings are prolonged F-wave and distal latencies and reduced CMAP amplitudes (p.3619).
Antiganglioside antibodies (e.g., anti-GM1 in AMAN/AMSAN, anti-GQ1b in Miller Fisher) can support specific subtypes (p.3618-3619).
Test for HIV in patients with risk factors or CSF pleocytosis (p.3620).
redFlags: Rapid tempo of progression and severe weakness on admission, plus facial and/or bulbar weakness in the first week, predict the need for mechanical ventilation (up to ~30% of patients require ventilatory support) (p.3617).
Bulbar weakness with difficulty handling secretions threatens the airway (p.3617).
Autonomic instability - wide blood pressure swings, postural hypotension, and cardiac dysrhythmias - can be fatal and may occur even when limb weakness is otherwise mild (p.3617).
Presence of fever or constitutional symptoms at onset casts doubt on the diagnosis and should prompt reconsideration (p.3617).
Prominent or early bladder dysfunction, or a sensory level, should raise suspicion for spinal cord disease rather than GBS (p.3617).
harrison.prognosis: About 85% of patients reach full functional recovery within several months to a year, though minor signs (e.g., persistent areflexia) and complaints such as fatigue may remain. Mortality is <5% in optimal settings, usually from secondary pulmonary complications. The outlook is worst with severe proximal motor and sensory axonal damage; other adverse factors are advanced age, a fulminant or severe attack, and delayed treatment. Elevated serum neurofilament light chains and high anti-GM1 titers both correlate with greater axonal involvement and poorer recovery. Between 5 and 10% of typical GBS patients have one or more late relapses, many later reclassified as CIDP (p.3621-3622).
pitfalls: Corticosteroids have NOT been found effective in GBS and should not be relied on as treatment (p.3621).

Treatment timing matters: each day counts, and by ~2 weeks after the first motor symptoms it is unknown whether immunotherapy is still effective; if a patient has reached the plateau, treatment is probably no longer indicated unless severe weakness suggests ongoing immune attack (p.3620).
Lack of improvement after a course of IVIg or plasmapheresis is NOT an indication to switch to the other modality, and combining the two is not significantly better than either alone (p.3621).
Early CSF and electrodiagnostic studies can be normal/minimal; relying on them to confirm before treating can cause harmful delay (p.3619-3620).
Acute flaccid myelitis can closely mimic GBS because sphincter disturbances may be absent (p.3620).
harrison.severityClassification: Brighton Collaboration case definitions (2011) grade diagnostic certainty in three levels. Level 1 (highest certainty) requires bilateral flaccid limb weakness, decreased/absent reflexes in weak limbs, a monophasic course with onset-to-nadir of 12 h to 28 days followed by plateau, electrophysiology consistent with GBS, cytoalbuminologic dissociation (elevated CSF protein with CSF white cell count <50/microL), and no alternative diagnosis. Lower levels relax the laboratory/electrophysiologic requirements. Parallel criteria exist for Miller Fisher syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia without limb weakness) (p.3620-3621).
